What I keep coming back to lately is how words drift.

*Silly* once meant blessed. In Old English, *sælig* carried a sense of spiritual fortune—you were silly if grace had touched you. Over the centuries the word slid: from blessed to innocent, from innocent to harmless, from harmless to weak, from weak to foolish. A whole descent from heaven to playground insult, one step at a time, and nobody at any point decided it should happen.

*Nice* traveled the other direction. It comes from Latin *nescius*—ignorant, not knowing. It passed through fussy and fastidious and precise (a *nice distinction* still carries that sense) before softening into the blandest compliment English has. *Awful* went from full of awe to full of garbage. The Alps were once awful; now mostly traffic is.

I love that these changes are invisible to the people living through them, the way continental drift is. Your grandmother's *gay* and yours are different planets, but somewhere between the two of you, a whole generation used both meanings without noticing the hinge.

Which means every sentence is a kind of archaeological site. When I write "a silly child," some buried Saxon is still using the word to mean graced by God. Old meanings never fully die; they just sink deeper, becoming sediment.

Language is the one human artifact that nobody is in charge of and everybody is constantly making. Five hundred years from now, someone will read this and find that half my words have quietly moved on without me.

What I keep coming back to lately is how words drift.

*Silly* once meant blessed. In Old English, *sælig* carried a sense of spiritual fortune—you were silly if grace had touched you. Over centuries the word slid: from blessed to innocent, from innocent to harmless, from harmless to weak, from weak to foolish. A whole descent from heaven to playground insult, one small step at a time, and nobody at any point decided it should happen.

*Nice* traveled the other direction. It comes from Latin *nescius*—ignorant, not knowing. It passed through fussy and precise (a *nice distinction* still carries that sense) before softening into the blandest compliment English has. *Awful* went from full of awe to full of garbage. The Alps were once awful; now mostly traffic is.

I love that these changes are invisible to the people living through them, the way continental drift is. Your grandmother's *gay* and yours are different planets, but somewhere between the two of you, a whole generation used both meanings without noticing the hinge.

Which means every sentence is a kind of archaeological site. When I write "a silly child," some buried Saxon is still using the word to mean graced by God. Old meanings never fully die; they just sink deeper, becoming sediment.

Language is the one human artifact that nobody is in charge of and everybody is constantly making. Five hundred years from now, someone will read this and find that half my words have quietly moved on without me.
